issues.legal_issue: A court may extend time for payment stipulated in a compromise when the parties invited the court to incorporate the compromise into its order and no statutory rule compelled a particular outcome in the underlying proceeding absent the compromise.
material_facts: A sale in execution of a money decree was set aside on appeal, and the decree-holder challenged that decision in a further appeal.
The parties compromised during the further appeal, with the court’s leave, and the court made an order in terms of their compromise.
The compromise required payment by a specified time and provided for an adverse outcome if payment was not made by then.
After failing to pay on time, the judgment debtors applied to extend the time for payment.
The High Court dismissed the application on the view that it lacked power to extend a period fixed by the parties.
Without the compromise, the court would have decided the appeal on its merits; it was not statutorily compelled to dismiss the challenge to the sale.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had power to extend the time because the parties’ stipulated time became time allowed by the court when their compromise was incorporated into its order. Such an extension is not ordinary or available merely on request; it may be granted in rare cases to prevent manifest injustice. Whether an extension should be granted on these facts was left for the High Court to decide.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 148 and 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a court may extend time in an appropriate case where the time fixed by the parties in a compromise has merged into an order of the court. The court’s ability to further the ends of justice is not curtailed by the parties’ contract, and it may relieve against a forfeiture clause in a rare case to prevent manifest injustice. Hukumchand v. Bansilal was distinguishable: there, dismissal of the application to set aside the sale triggered a statutory compulsion to confirm the sale, so further postponement depended on the parties’ consent; here, absent the compromise, the underlying appeal would have been decided on its merits.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge_appeal and parties_compromise_incorporated_into_court_order and no_mandatory_outcome_without_compromise and payment_time_expired and extension_requested

predicates.execution_sale_challenge_appeal: The proceeding concerns an appeal arising from a challenge to a sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.parties_compromise_incorporated_into_cou: The parties agreed on a compromise and invited the court to make an order in its terms.
predicates.no_mandatory_outcome_without_compromise: Without the compromise, the court was free to decide the underlying proceeding on its merits rather than being required by law to impose a particular outcome.
predicates.payment_time_expired: The time for payment set out in the compromise and court order passed without payment being made.
predicates.extension_requested: A party asked the court to allow more time for payment.

issues.definition: When an execution-sale challenge is still to be decided on its merits absent a compromise, the parties’ compromise is incorporated into a court order, the payment deadline passes, and an extension is requested, the court has power to extend time in an appropriate case.
